questions.q: What indexing pattern does SQL Server's DiskANN preview favor, and why?
options: Continuous trickle writes against a live vector index, because it is always fresh
Index-after-load: bulk ingest first, then build the index once — rather than fighting continuous trickle writes against an existing vector index
Dropping and recreating the table on every row change
Storing vectors only in memory with no persisted index
questions.explain: SQL Server's DiskANN index in preview favors an index-after-load pattern — bulk ingest into the table first, then CREATE VECTOR INDEX once — over continuous trickle writes; buffer writes and rebuild on a schedule the freshness SLA requires.

questions.q: What is the role of the ContentHash guard in the embedding generation pipeline?
options: It compresses chunk text before sending it to the embedding API
It shards documents across workers
It encrypts the embedding vectors at rest
It is the pipeline's idempotency key: re-running on an unchanged document updates nothing, so the job is safely re-runnable and the embedding API is never billed twice for the same text
questions.explain: The ContentHash guard makes ingestion idempotent — a re-run on unchanged documents updates nothing, so the pipeline is safely re-runnable and never double-bills the embedding API.

questions.q: Which change-capture approach matches which freshness SLA, and what must both handle explicitly?
options: Neither approach can detect deletes, so ghost content is unavoidable
CDC for minutes-level, watermark polling for sub-minute; both must handle schema changes
Watermark polling for minutes-level freshness, SQL Server CDC for sub-minute; both must handle deletes explicitly or the index serves ghost content
Triggers for both SLAs; deletes are handled automatically by the vector index
questions.explain: Watermark polling suits minutes-level freshness and CDC suits sub-minute; in both approaches a deleted source document must delete its chunks, or the vector index keeps serving ghost content.

questions.q: What is the stage-and-swap backfill pattern for large datasets?
options: Backfill into a staging table, build the DiskANN index on it, validate recall on the canary set, then switch the app via synonym repointing or a view in one transaction — the old table is the instant rollback
Backfill directly into production and hope the index rebuilds itself
Skip backfill and re-embed everything on every query
Backfill into the live table row by row with no index
questions.explain: Stage, then swap: new table, new index, canary-validated, synonym-switched in one transaction, with the old table as instant rollback and checkpointed batches throughout.

questions.q: How do you distinguish recall degradation caused by index staleness from corpus drift?
options: A falling recall@k trend after heavy ingest periods means rebuild the DiskANN index; a falling trend with no ingest correlation points at corpus drift — new topics the chunking or model handles poorly
Both are fixed by increasing MAXDOP
Run DBCC CHECKDB to tell them apart
They cannot be distinguished; always rebuild first
questions.explain: The canary diagnostic: falling recall@k after heavy ingest signals a needed index rebuild, while a falling trend with no ingest correlation points at corpus drift.
